# Part A: Influence walkthrough on `savings` (11:40-12:10)

The `savings` data: average savings rate (`sr`, % of disposable income) for 50
countries, 1960-1970, with age structure (`pop15`, `pop75`), per-capita
disposable income (`dpi`), and income growth (`ddpi`). Country names are the
row names. This is the most famous influence example in the regression
literature; by the end you will know why.

## A1. Fit the model

```{r}
#| eval: false
g <- lm(sr ~ pop15 + pop75 + dpi + ddpi, data = savings)
summary(g)
```

**Which coefficients are statistically significant at the 5% level? Fill in:
the `ddpi` coefficient is ____, meaning each additional point of income growth
is associated with ____ points ____ (higher/lower) average savings rate,
holding the other three variables fixed, among these 50 countries.** ...

## A2. Leverage: who has unusual predictors?

Leverage (hat value) $h_i$ measures how extreme country $i$'s predictor
profile is. The average must be $p/n$; values above $2p/n$ deserve a look.

```{r}
#| eval: false
h <- hatvalues(g)

n <- ___          # number of countries
p <- ___          # number of coefficients (count the intercept!)
c(average_leverage = p / n, flag_threshold = 2 * p / n)

sort(h, decreasing = TRUE)[1:5]
halfnorm(h, labs = row.names(savings), ylab = "Leverage")
```

**Which two countries exceed the threshold? For the top one, look at its row
(`savings["___", ]`) and compare to `summary(savings$ddpi)`: which predictor
makes it extreme?** ...

## A3. Outliers: who has a surprising savings rate?

Studentized residuals re-estimate the error SD without each observation, so a
big outlier cannot dilute its own evidence. With 50 countries we examine the
biggest of 50 residuals, so we use the Bonferroni-corrected cutoff.

```{r}
#| eval: false
rst <- rstudent(g)
sort(abs(rst), decreasing = TRUE)[1:3]

qt(1 - 0.05 / (2 * n), df = n - p - 1)   # Bonferroni critical value
```

**Which country has the largest studentized residual, and is it a formal
outlier by the Bonferroni standard? One sentence.** ...

## A4. Influence: who actually moves the fit?

```{r}
#| eval: false
ck <- cooks.distance(g)
sort(ck, decreasing = TRUE)[1:3]
halfnorm(ck, 3, labs = row.names(savings), ylab = "Cook's distance")
```

**The top Cook's distance country: is it the same as the top-leverage country,
the top-outlier country, both, or neither? Explain using D = (residual part)
x (leverage part).** ...

## A5. Refit without the top influential country

```{r}
#| eval: false
g_drop <- lm(sr ~ pop15 + pop75 + dpi + ddpi, data = savings,
             subset = row.names(savings) != "___")
round(rbind(full = coef(g), dropped = coef(g_drop)), 4)
```

Fill in the comparison:

- The coefficient that changes most in relative terms is ____, moving from
  ____ to ____ (a change of roughly ____ %).
- The sign of every coefficient (does / does not) stay the same.
- One sentence you could write in a paper reporting this sensitivity check: ...

# Part B: The pathology hunt (12:50-13:25, in pairs)

Each of the four variants below draws a fresh sample of 50 counties and (in
three of the four) plants exactly one anomaly in row 50. **One variant is
completely clean.** You get one variant; you do not know in advance which kind
you drew.

Run this chunk as-is, then set your variant from your pair number.

```{r}
#| label: make-variant
make_variant <- function(variant) {
  stopifnot(variant %in% 0:3)
  pool <- county_health |>
    drop_na(uninsured, poverty) |>
    filter(between(poverty, 5, 22), between(uninsured, 3, 22))
  seeds <- c(69, 3, 7, 13)
  set.seed(seeds[variant + 1])
  d <- pool |> slice_sample(n = 50) |> select(state, name, uninsured, poverty)
  if (variant == 1) { d$poverty[50] <- 45; d$uninsured[50] <- 19.75 }
  if (variant == 2) { d$uninsured[50] <- d$uninsured[50] + 22 }
  if (variant == 3) { d$poverty[50] <- 50; d$uninsured[50] <- 2 }
  d
}
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
pair_number <- ___          # from the board
variant <- pair_number %% 4
my_counties <- make_variant(variant)
```

(Yes, the planting code is visible above. The exercise is to *demonstrate with
diagnostics* what was planted and what it does to the model, exactly as you
would for an anomaly nobody planted on purpose.)
